inputs: Verified DCM and intermediary status, current contract specifications and rulebooks, settlement sources, dispute provisions, trading hours, market-data licenses, API terms, geographic restrictions, and written builder or referral arrangements where offered.

Timestamped executable bids and offers, displayed depth, trades, venue and intermediary fees, rate limits, account-access architecture, and contract taxonomies that preserve differences in event definitions, observation windows, and settlement rules.

A documented activity analysis covering compensated solicitation, order acceptance or transmission, personalized recommendations, discretionary trading, IB/FCM/CTA requirements and available exemptions; scoped API permissions, consent records, commercial disclosures, and an explicit prohibition on custody and pooled capital.
operator_plays.mechanism: Earn subscriptions from cross-venue probability, settlement-rule, and liquidity analytics for event contracts listed on CFTC Designated Contract Markets such as Kalshi and ForecastEx, using licensed data and venue-authorized access channels. Add builder or referral compensation only where the relevant exchange, intermediary, and applicable registration framework permit the specific activity; non-custody alone does not remove introducing-broker or commodity-trading-advisor obligations. Keep customer funds, positions, margin, and account approval with the authorized venue or intermediary, and use read-only analytics or permitted outbound referrals unless order transmission has a documented lawful operating basis.
metrics: Subscription contribution margin = collected recurring revenue minus licensed data, infrastructure, support, payment processing, and acquisition costs; report referral receipts separately and net of contractual reversals.

Market-data quality: quote age, feed uptime, contract-mapping exception rate, and executable depth at the displayed price; calculate cross-venue spreads after all observable fees and explicit settlement-basis adjustments.

For authorized routing only, user-consented order acceptance rate, execution slippage against the timestamped executable quote, cancellation latency, and reconciliation exceptions; for referrals, verified attributed accounts and realized revenue per eligible referral.

platform_risks.detection_metric: Track feature and compensation changes against the documented permitted-activity scope, percentage of order endpoints with an established authorization basis, and unresolved venue-term or registration-status exceptions.
platform_risks.failure_mode: A non-custodial analytics product crosses into compensated solicitation, order handling, or advisory activity without the required registration or a valid exemption.
platform_risks.fallback: Disable the affected routing, solicitation, or recommendation feature, preserve records, and continue only the lawfully supported read-only analytics or referral functionality; resume expanded activity through an appropriately registered arrangement or a substantiated exemption.
platform_risks.impact: Routing suspension, terminated commercial agreements, regulatory exposure, customer execution disputes, and loss of referral revenue despite the platform never holding funds.
platform_risks.trigger: A builder integration begins transmitting customer orders, transaction-linked compensation changes the solicitation model, personalized trade recommendations are introduced, or venue and intermediary terms change.

workflow: 1. Confirm each venue's current regulatory status, customer-access model, data rights, and permitted territories; distinguish direct venue access from intermediary access, including ForecastEx access through authorized intermediaries, and verify the current availability of any commercial referral program.

2. Normalize contracts only when their event definitions and settlement mechanics support a meaningful comparison; display bid/ask-derived implied probabilities, depth, timestamps, fees, and settlement differences rather than describing every price spread as executable arbitrage.

3. Launch paid read-only dashboards with stale-data suppression, spread and depth filters, reproducible calculations, and clearly disclosed commercial relationships; assess whether recommendation features create CTA obligations before enabling them.

4. Enable only contractually permitted referral links or a separately authorized routing implementation after documenting the registration or exemption basis; require user-directed orders through the authorized venue or intermediary, minimize token permissions, and retain consent and routing logs without receiving customer funds.

inputs: A current jurisdiction-by-product authorization matrix covering operator licenses, affiliate or vendor requirements, permitted compensation models, marketing restrictions, minimum ages, and Ontario AGCO and iGaming Ontario requirements relevant to each participant's role.

Executed operator agreements defining eligible first-time depositors, identity and location verification, qualifying deposits or wagering, attribution windows, CPA reversals, NGR deductions, revenue-share percentages, negative-carryover scope, payment timing, and audit or reconciliation rights.

Versioned comparison data, operator-confirmed product availability, consent-based attribution, location and age-screening controls, responsible-gambling resources, suppression and self-exclusion handling where applicable, and editorial rules excluding offshore operators and unlawful sweepstakes destinations.
operator_plays.mechanism: Operate jurisdiction-specific sportsbook and online-casino comparison calculators and matchup hubs that route eligible adults only to operators authorized for the relevant product and location in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Michigan, West Virginia, or Ontario, which is a Canadian province rather than a US state. Earn contractually verified first-time-depositor CPA and, where permitted, negotiated net-gaming-revenue shares after specified bonus, tax, administrative, chargeback, and negative-carryover treatment. Obtain the affiliate, vendor, supplier, or revenue-share permissions actually required in each jurisdiction and commercial arrangement; do not assume one registration covers every market or compensation model.
metrics: Realized CPA yield = paid, non-reversed CPA revenue divided by eligible referred visitors; track click-to-registration, verified registration-to-qualifying-depositor conversion, rejection reasons, and the lag between acquisition and cash collection.

Realized revenue share = contractual share percentage applied to the eligible NGR base after agreed deductions and carryover treatment; reconcile the opening negative balance, current-period activity, payable amount, and closing balance by contractual reporting unit.

Jurisdiction-level contribution margin and control quality: content and acquisition cost per paid depositor, cash payback period, blocked ineligible-location clicks, age-screening failures, outdated offers, and operator-authorization exceptions.
operator_plays.name: NJ, PA, MI, WV and Ontario Regulated Gaming Affiliate Comparison Desk

platform_risks.detection_metric: Monitor restricted-location link exposure, unauthorized destination counts, jurisdiction-specific advertising exceptions, CPA reversal rates, and unexplained differences between internal estimates and operator settlement statements.
platform_risks.failure_mode: A comparison page routes an ineligible visitor or publishes an impermissible promotion, while weak reconciliation overstates earnings from rejected depositors or negative NGR.
platform_risks.fallback: Disable affected offers and monetized links by jurisdiction, preserve relevant records, replace promotional content with permitted factual information, and reconcile or dispute settlement differences through contractual processes; never redirect blocked traffic to offshore operators or unlawful sweepstakes.
platform_risks.impact: Affiliate suspension, withheld commissions, regulatory action, customer harm, and materially lower cash receipts than the portal's gross acquisition dashboard suggests.
platform_risks.trigger: Location cannot be verified, an operator loses or changes authorization, a public Ontario page displays a prohibited inducement, or operator reporting applies unexpected bonus deductions, clawbacks, or carryover.

workflow: 1. Build separate NJ, PA, MI, WV, and Ontario inventories, verify operator and affiliate permissions for sportsbook versus casino activity, and complete any required registrations before monetizing the relevant traffic; require age 21 in the four listed US states and age 19 in Ontario.

2. Publish substantiated comparisons and matchup content with prominent affiliate disclosures, clear calculator assumptions, and responsible-gambling information; apply jurisdiction-specific promotion rules, including Ontario restrictions on public advertising of gambling inducements, bonuses, and credits.

3. Restrict monetized links to eligible locations and products using layered geolocation and fail-closed handling of uncertain location, without offering circumvention instructions; use affiliate age screening while leaving mandatory identity, age, self-exclusion, and wagering-location verification with the authorized operator.

4. Reconcile operator-confirmed qualifying depositors, duplicate or fraudulent accounts, CPA clawbacks, and contract-defined monthly NGR; account for deductions and negative carryover at the agreed player, brand, product, or portfolio level, and suspend links immediately when authorization or permitted marketing terms change.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I connect to Kalshi, Polymarket and other prediction-market APIs and build my own terminals, assistants and AI trading bots on top of them?
chapters.title: Wiring the Terminal: Prediction-Market APIs, Dashboards & AI Bots
chapters.subtitle: Ranking prediction-market APIs, Kalshi Python tutorials, unifying Polymarket and Kalshi schemas, Perplexity Sonar assistants, Qwidgets order-book charts, Kalshi Pro terminal, OddsFantasy automation, and LLM-driven trading bots
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners wiring prediction-market terminals agree on a split stack: Kalshi for the regulated, KYC'd, fiat-funded US account with a free documented API, Polymarket for crypto-native volume that Part Time Larry pegs at at least ten times Kalshi's, and a normalization layer because the two venues share almost no IDs, field names, or order-book shapes. The street mechanics are concrete: 200-event cursor pages, cached SQLite scrapes, bearer-token websockets, fill-or-kill orders priced high to mimic market orders, and RSA keys kept in .env files. Predictify's free tier gives 25,000 credits and seven days of history; Builder costs $48.88 a month. Disagreement centers on whether to buy a cross-venue layer (Predictify versus Codex) and whether LLMs can trade at all: Part Time Larry and OngPredicts pipe model output toward order flow, while Three Markets watched AI portfolios bleed and suggested counter-trading them.

key_metrics.label: Predictify cross-venue coverage
key_metrics.value: 16 prediction-market venues through one normalized API
key_metrics.context: OngPredicts ranks Predictify first for cross-venue builders because it covers 16 venues including Polymarket and Kalshi, with market catalogs, order books, trades, candles, and live streams where supported.

key_metrics.value: $48.88 per month for 500,000 credits; free plan 25,000 credits and 7 days of history
key_metrics.context: The full OngPredicts tutorial (searches, books, comparison, history, 7-day backtest) cost 55 credits, so the free plan could run it more than 450 times; history past 7 days and the replay route start at Builder.

key_metrics.value: 193 seconds for 30,000 events cold; 1.5 seconds from cache
key_metrics.context: Part Time Larry's Streamlit assistant pages through roughly 30,000 Kalshi events with nested markets at 200 per request, then reloads instantly once the cache decorator holds the data.

key_metrics.label: Perplexity structured-output reliability
key_metrics.value: Works about 90% of the time

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Start with venue choice, because every practitioner frames the build around the same two rails. Robot Traders calls Kalshi the only CFTC-regulated prediction market platform in the US, notes it raised $1 billion at roughly a $22 billion valuation with 5 million monthly users, and stresses that its API is free and well documented [yYjo1lzNoGI @ 00:00:17]. Part Time Larry runs a funded Kalshi account after passing KYC with their ID, wires it to a normal bank account in fiat, and contrasts that with Polymarket's crypto element and unclear country-by-country legality, while conceding Polymarket carries at least ten times the volume and dominates the election odds quoted on TV and Twitter [E2mgWN4ReqQ @ 00:02:22]. Defined adds the settlement trade-off: Kalshi resolves on authoritative official sources, which helps compliance and user trust, but settlement can take from about an hour to more than 12 hours after close, while Polymarket geoblocks and runs a separate US-regulated product so global and US users see different catalogs [LefzH8sYzRI @ 00:07:39]. ShaunsTake states the motive plainly: after being limited to $5 on PrizePicks, banned on Dabble, and capped at $25 on Underdog, they moved to prediction markets as platforms that will not limit you for winning [A3KSnSZOPtM @ 00:09:42].

The second consensus point is that raw venue APIs do not speak the same language, so normalization is the real work. OngPredicts opens by saying Polymarket and Kalshi agree on almost nothing: Polymarket returns prices as a list packed inside a string beside two token IDs more than 70 digits long, while Kalshi returns a ticker with bid and ask written as dollar strings, and Kalshi's native book only sends bids, one list for yes and one for no, leaving you to derive asks [OEhjqCpa1Uw @ 00:00:32]. Part Time Larry hit the same wall from the research side, building a betting model that uses semantic matching because the wording of Fed rate-cut, payroll, Beyonce album, and China-Taiwan bets differs across venues [E2mgWN4ReqQ @ 00:04:04]. Defined ranks Codex first precisely because it eliminates stitching together venue-native APIs, normalizing symbols, IDs, and resolution statuses into one GraphQL-style schema with websockets across Polymarket and Kalshi [LefzH8sYzRI @ 00:03:24]. OngPredicts' own countdown lands on Predictify for the same reason: 16 venues through one normalized API, plus grouping of equivalent markets so a builder can ask where a question is trading rather than designing around whichever venue they integrated first [HtGMBJ7ynjs @ 00:04:13].

Every serious builder also agrees that a price gap is a pointer, not a trade, and that resolution rules decide everything. OngPredicts pulled the Dan Sullivan Alaska Senate market at 26 and 27 cents on Polymarket versus 23 and 24 on Kalshi, a 3-cent gap that looks like buying yes at 24 and no at 74 for 98 cents against a $1 payout, but Predictify labeled it an indicative comparison and judged the markets not equivalent because they differ on who decides the result and how the deadline is handled, before fees and real share depth even enter [OEhjqCpa1Uw @ 00:04:29]. Part Time Larry learned it on a 41-cent test bet: they bet three Fed cuts in 2024, lost, because the 25, 25, and 50 basis-point moves counted as four cuts under Kalshi's rules, and now insists you read the rules or have the LLM read them [Ib0BEFKAvn0 @ 00:13:30]. Three Markets caught Grok trading a Google most-searched market without ever checking the resolution criteria or the data methodology that made the title misleading [iL5j83SC_fg @ 00:07:20]. BetSmart repeats Better Odds' warning that heavy resting money on one side does not mean sharp money until you identify the wallet behind it [jauhFM_n5d4 @ 00:02:30].

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The raw Kalshi pipeline is short and both Python teachers build it the same way. Part Time Larry hits the trade API v2 events endpoint with plain HTTP requests, passes with nested markets equal to true, filters status to open, and sets limit to 200, the ceiling per page, then walks the cursor until it runs dry; requests-cache stores every response in a local SQLite database so overnight scrapes restart where they failed, tqdm shows progress, and each day's markets are dumped to a timestamped JSON file and read into a pandas DataFrame [E2mgWN4ReqQ @ 00:09:05]. For live data they post username and password to get a token, send it as a Bearer header on the websocket, and subscribe to orderbook delta, ticker, trade, or fill channels [E2mgWN4ReqQ @ 00:15:11]. Robot Traders runs the official SDK installed with pip install kalshi python sync on Python 3.13 and finds recurring markets by walking series to events to markets: filtering series by category crypto returned 225 series, and the series ticker locks onto each new BTC 15-minute market without code changes [yYjo1lzNoGI @ 00:07:22]. From the market ticker they pull the order book's first 10 levels, best yes bid and ask, spread, midpoint, and recent trades [yYjo1lzNoGI @ 00:09:49].

Execution is where the tricks live. Robot Traders generates the key under account security, picks read and write because read-only only fetches balance-style data, downloads the RSA private key as a .pem file, and loads both through a .env so the code can be shared with an AI agent without leaking secrets; a balance call returning 25.13 confirms the handshake [yYjo1lzNoGI @ 00:12:10]. Kalshi has no true market orders, so they mimic one with a fill-or-kill limit order and a deliberately high yes price, converting a dollar stake into contract count by dividing it by the current ask; resting good-till-canceled limits take the price in cents divided by 100 and are cancelled by order ID pulled from get orders [yYjo1lzNoGI @ 00:13:41]. Part Time Larry's assistant shows the AI layer in 100 lines: Streamlit caches the 30,000-event load, a keyword and category filter builds a markdown context, and Perplexity's Sonar reasoning model returns a Pydantic schema of ticker, side, bid price, reason, and a 0-to-100 confidence score that could feed an order call directly [Ib0BEFKAvn0 @ 00:21:32]. OngPredicts' JEV bot skips unless data is fresh, edge survives fees, liquidity is sufficient, and the trade fits a $10 cap, then sizes positions on confirmed fills only [kDOrvOpgzjE @ 00:03:40].

The packaged stacks come with hard numbers. Quantitative Predictions prices Predictify's free tier at 25,000 credits a month and 60 requests per minute, with history replays for backtesting reserved for the pro plan [AoLKXHhSRtM @ 00:06:28], against Sports Game Odds' $149 entry plan and a $500 pro tier still capped at 300 requests per minute with only sub-minute updates [AoLKXHhSRtM @ 00:04:27]. OngPredicts itemizes the Predictify credit meter: search costs 1 credit, an order book 5, a cross-venue comparison 10, and history 5 per venue, so the full tutorial burned 55 credits; the free key stops at 7 days of history and returns 403 plan required past that, while Builder at $48.88 a month buys 500,000 credits, 12 months of history, and a replay route where 47,000 Kalshi quotes cost 16 credits [OEhjqCpa1Uw @ 00:07:59]. OddsFantasy's no-code home-favorite preset buys moneyline yes on the home team between 1.25 and 1.8 odds with spread under 0.05, stakes $5 per market, sets a 50% drawdown control, runs from one hour before kickoff on a 2-minute refresh and stops right after kickoff, then previews which matches pass the entry rules before choosing live or limit-quote execution [s_VGmKtzL-0 @ 00:02:31].

callout.title: Small Wiring Moves That Save Money and Credits
callout.body: The builders who ship working terminals lean on caching, replay, execution workarounds and noise filters before they ever touch strategy.
items: Mimic a market order on Kalshi with fill-or-kill plus an aggressive yes price, because true market orders do not exist on the venue [Robot Traders — yYjo1lzNoGI @ 00:13:41]

Cache the catalog: the 30,000-event load took 193 seconds cold and 1.5 seconds from the Streamlit cache, but add an invalidation rule because odds keep moving [Part Time Larry — Ib0BEFKAvn0 @ 00:16:21]
Pull quotes once and replay from disk: nearly 47,000 Kalshi quotes over 28 days cost 16 credits and now replay for free while you iterate on code [OngPredicts — OEhjqCpa1Uw @ 00:06:56]
Strip the three biggest prints before reading tape: a 55-45 split is not a signal, and a real one looks like 85-15 or 90-10 on one side [ShaunsTake — A3KSnSZOPtM @ 00:04:31]

sop_steps.title: Provision keys and secrets
sop_steps.action: Create a read-and-write Kalshi API key, save the RSA private key as a .pem, and load both from a .env file.
sop_steps.detail: Read-only keys only fetch account data; placing bets needs read and write, and keeping keys outside the code lets you hand scripts to an AI agent safely. Verify with a balance call before trading [Robot Traders — yYjo1lzNoGI @ 00:12:10]

sop_steps.title: Build the cached market catalog
sop_steps.action: Page the events endpoint at 200 per request with nested markets, cache to SQLite, and save a dated JSON snapshot.
sop_steps.detail: Use requests-cache so long scrapes restart where they failed, then load the daily file into pandas for filtering by title or ticker instead of re-hitting the API [Part Time Larry — E2mgWN4ReqQ @ 00:10:09]

sop_steps.title: Normalize and qualify cross-venue gaps
sop_steps.action: Run matched markets through a comparison that checks resolution equivalence, fees and depth before treating a gap as tradable.
sop_steps.detail: A 3-cent Alaska Senate gap was flagged not equivalent because the venues differ on who decides the result and how the deadline is handled [OngPredicts — OEhjqCpa1Uw @ 00:04:11]

sop_steps.title: Dry-run the bot with hard caps
sop_steps.action: Set a $10 trading cap, run in dry-run mode, and read the logs before enabling live trades.
sop_steps.detail: Confirm the logs show the data snapshot, the model's estimate, and the reason for every trade or skip, then keep stakes small once live [OngPredicts — kDOrvOpgzjE @ 00:03:22]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: OngPredicts and Quantitative Predictions both crown Predictify as the cross-venue foundation, with OngPredicts pitching 16 prediction market venues through one normalized API as the real starting point for a serious cross-venue product [HtGMBJ7ynjs @ 00:03:51], and Quantitative Predictions naming Kalshi, Polymarket, Polymarket US, Novig, Gemini, Opinion and Hyperliquid among the covered venues [AoLKXHhSRtM @ 00:05:14]. Defined runs a different board: Codex takes number one as the best cross-venue API for multi-venue odds and trading, Polymarket is the best native DeFi API, and Kalshi is the best US regulated centralized API [LefzH8sYzRI @ 00:01:47]. Defined also cuts against the aggregator thesis for single-venue builds, arguing that a Polymarket-first terminal should go straight to the native API for the lowest latency and the richest access to venue-specific features [LefzH8sYzRI @ 00:05:53]. The countdowns split on the middle of the list too. OngPredicts slots Monit at number three as an agent-first tool marketplace whose prediction market foundation depends on which underlying tools you pick, while Quantitative Predictions drops it to fifth and keeps it only for fast onboarding, no subscription and roughly 2 cents per call. Quantitative Predictions also calls Nansen's Polymarket endpoints very basic and largely available on Polymarket's own API, where OngPredicts sells Nansen as a compelling toolkit for following wallets and studying trader behavior.

The AI layer is where the practitioners diverge hardest. Part Time Larry wires Perplexity's Sonar reasoning API to Kalshi with a Pydantic schema that returns side, ticker, bid price, reason and a 0 to 100 confidence score, and rates Grok as the sharper analyst because it is opinionated and willing to speculate where Gemini and OpenAI typically refuse and push you toward a financial advisor [Ib0BEFKAvn0 @ 00:07:03]. OngPredicts goes the other direction with Jeff from Typecase AI, a system one model that skips the essay entirely: you hand it the possible answers up front and it picks one with its own odds and a confidence score, costing 4.2 cents per million tokens read and nothing for what it answers [kDOrvOpgzjE @ 00:01:20]. Inside Prediction Markets keeps AI on the infrastructure and research side, with every engineer on a Claude Max plan writing multi-service trading systems, while the trading partner dumps the desk's fills from the database into Claude to diagnose why they are getting crushed in a specific market [gOWvAiqg_qw @ 00:15:57]. Three Markets is the skeptic of the group, arguing that resolution nuance and soft knowledge, such as Spotify filtering botted listens out of a chart market, is the kind of thing an AI cannot do super well and where humans still hold the edge [iL5j83SC_fg @ 00:02:13].

Order-flow reading splits the room into believers and skeptics. Handsome Finance builds a whale-following stack: Ashdav to filter trades above $10,000 and score traders, Polymarket Analytics to rank top wallets, and TradeFox to paste an address and copy all trades, for example allocating $50 to a test account mirrored at 100% [4sCGelTkwek @ 00:05:41]. The same channel watches deposits above $100k, reasoning that a big deposit precedes a big trade and the operator wants to know why [4sCGelTkwek @ 00:06:24]. ShaunsTake is warier with a free tapeline Discord bot, saying a good tape signal looks like 90-10 or 85-15 on one side, while the Cowboys over 9.5 spread tested on camera showed only 55% to 45% once the top three trades were stripped out as possible hedges or arbitrage [A3KSnSZOPtM @ 00:04:31]. BetSmart flags the same limit inside the Better Odds terminal: a one-sided book shows resting money on one position but does not prove sharp money, because the owner's wallet has not been identified, so the play is to use the imbalance to line shop recreational sportsbooks for expected value [jauhFM_n5d4 @ 00:02:43]. Even Handsome Finance passes on a wallet showing $2 million in profit after judging it to be a bot farming arbitrage rather than a trader worth copying.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap is treating a price gap as a trade. OngPredicts lined up the Dan Sullivan Alaska Senate race at 26 to 27 cents on Polymarket and 23 to 24 cents on Kalshi, then read the verdict underneath: an indicative comparison only, with the two markets judged not equivalent because they differ on who decides the result and how the deadline is handled [OEhjqCpa1Uw @ 00:04:11]. On paper, yes on Kalshi at 24 and no on Polymarket at 74 costs 98 cents for something paying a dollar, but it only pays if both venues settle on the same result, and that is before fees on both sides and before checking how many shares really sit at those prices [OEhjqCpa1Uw @ 00:04:29]. Part Time Larry got burned on rules at test size: a 41-cent bet on three Fed cuts in 2024 lost because the 25, 25 and 50 basis point sequence counted as four cuts under the contract rules, so you or the LLM must read the rules before trading [Ib0BEFKAvn0 @ 00:13:30]. Three Markets caught the same failure inside the AI arena, where Grok bet no on a Google most-searched-people market without ever going to the resolution criteria or the data methodology behind a misleading title [iL5j83SC_fg @ 00:07:20].

Backtests and pricing tiers are where unit economics bite. OngPredicts ran a dip-buying rule on the free plan's seven days and got zero finished trades, and asking for 30 days on a free key returns 403 plan required rather than quietly shortening the window [OEhjqCpa1Uw @ 00:06:17]. On a paid key the same rule read 73 candles per venue, closed three trades and lost $4 because the price drifted down while it kept buying the dip; the stricter replay on Kalshi quotes, filling only a quarter of shown size and paying Kalshi's fees, took 12 to 18 fills per 100-share order and came out at minus $6.77, with $4.27 of that going to fees [OEhjqCpa1Uw @ 00:07:35]. Quantitative Predictions warns that Monit's per-call pricing is cheap to start but adds up very quickly once you are copy trading or running an actual bot [AoLKXHhSRtM @ 00:01:06], and slams the Sports Game Odds pro plan, where $500 still buys only sub-minute updates when you would hope for sub-second on prediction market data, with $149 as the cheapest paid tier [AoLKXHhSRtM @ 00:04:27]. Predictify's builder plan, the tier that unlocks 12 months of history and the replay route, runs $48.88 a month with 500,000 credits.

Live bots fail on plumbing before they fail on picks. Part Time Larry found Perplexity's structured outputs work about 90% of the time, sometimes nesting results under a contracts key, sometimes returning a bare list, sometimes wrapping the JSON in backticks, which forced string juggling before any order could be built [Ib0BEFKAvn0 @ 00:22:52]. A rerun of the same Democratic nominee payload then flipped Mark Cuban to undervalued and added Buttigieg at 6 cents, which is why the build stayed an assistant instead of an agent told to bet $20 [Ib0BEFKAvn0 @ 00:25:05]. OngPredicts designs around partial fills, noting that requested size and filled size can differ, so the Jeff bot books positions only on confirmed fills and skips any round where data freshness, post-fee edge, liquidity or the $10 cap fails [kDOrvOpgzjE @ 00:04:02]. ShaunsTake's day-one tape bot returned insufficient recent activity even on a busier Bitcoin strike, either a bug or a thin market still waiting on a fix [A3KSnSZOPtM @ 00:08:24]. Three Markets watched the leading LLMs, each handed $10,000, burning it, with Deep Seek down 10% as the best performer and Gemini holding yes on DraftKings launching a prediction market in 2025.

callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, a bug or a near miss a practitioner hit on camera. Clear all four before a bot or a cross-venue pair goes live.

chapters.question_prompt: How do operators find and execute arbitrage and speed-based edges across prediction markets and sportsbooks, and why do slow feeds kill the trade?
chapters.title: Cross-Venue Arbitrage & the Latency Problem
chapters.subtitle: Kalshi–Polymarket arbitrage tools, 15+ venue arb terminals and phantom price gaps, ChatGPT-built arb bots, free AI arb scanners, OddsJam arbitrage and live betting, sportsbook-vs-Kalshi pricing strategies, and why ESPN-fed NFL bots and live-betting latency lose
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree the cross-venue trade is simple: buy YES on one prediction market and NO on another for a combined cost under $1, favoring Kalshi and Polymarket because peer-to-peer, fee-funded exchanges do not limit arbers the way sportsbooks do. On mechanics, Predictify runs $48.88 a month across 15-plus venues, arbs.xyz $997 a year, and Chen Trading's $100 Mark Kelly pair showed an estimated $7.75 net after roughly 94 cents in fees once book depth was walked. Latency is the hard ceiling: Part Time Larry's ESPN-fed Kalshi bot scratched at break-even as Kalshi moved before the free signal, pro feeds run near $5,000 a month, and Whale Slots puts consumer streams 7 to 30 seconds behind. The live disagreement is whether scanner gaps are real: OngPredicts traced every top gap they rechecked to a dead or already-moved venue price.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every arbitrage operator here runs the same core trade: find one event listed on two venues, buy YES on one and NO on the other, and confirm the two prices add up to less than $1, because exactly one leg settles at $1 and the gap is locked profit. Taf frames it with a 35-cent YES on Polymarket plus a 40-cent NO on Kalshi for 75 cents total, leaving a 25-cent spread that pays no matter which side resolves [GLvhRHB7n2U @ 00:02:45]. Juiced Bets runs the J.D. Vance illustration: YES at 60 on Kalshi, NO at 35 on Polymarket, 95 cents in for a guaranteed 100 cents back, a 5% return with zero view on the election [PaQjSUCZVb0 @ 00:03:05]. OngPredicts uses the same 40-plus-55 structure and stresses they do not care who wins as long as both legs cover every outcome and resolve the same way [to-RcU1_UCQ @ 00:01:13]. Scrape Atlas pitches 42 cents YES against 53 cents NO for 95 cents total and warns that platform take rates and likely payment processing fees must come out of that spread before it counts [OPiw3RZFInQ @ 00:01:54]. The shared prerequisite is blunt: price both legs, subtract fees, and only fire when the combined cost still clears under the $1 payout.

The second point of agreement is why arbers left sportsbooks. Taf says books clock arbitrage activity and limit accounts until you cannot bet anymore, which happened to Taf and many other bettors, while prediction markets carry no bans, no limits, and prices Taf calls extremely inefficient [GLvhRHB7n2U @ 00:00:50]. Clark Knows Ball explains the business model: Kalshi is peer-to-peer, you are filling another user's open order, and the exchange earns on every transaction, so it has no reason to cut a winner from hundreds or thousands per play down to five or ten dollars the way FanDuel or DraftKings do [ghCIWcXbadk @ 00:01:02]. Bet The Math says Kalshi and Polymarket never limit, never cut bet sizes, and actually love arbitrage bettors, so the strategy scales until it hits available liquidity, with arbs showing up both between two prediction markets and between a prediction market and a sportsbook [nOjpng5gNGo @ 00:07:14]. Juiced Bets confirms the platforms have no issue with arbitrage because they are not making money when you lose, only a fee on every trade [PaQjSUCZVb0 @ 00:00:46]. The caveat travels with the praise: that fee is the venue's revenue, so the no-limits pitch always arrives paired with fee math on each leg.

On live markets, the consensus is blunt: the retail viewer is the slowest node in the chain. Part Time Larry watched ESPN's Gamecast log a Walker touchdown while the TV stream still showed Seattle scoreless, cited a 5-to-15-second Gamecast lead over broadcast and a 15-to-30-second lag on free data versus pro feeds that might run $5,000 a month, and concluded that tapping bets on a phone mid-game gets you 'the worst odds you could possibly have' [bA_NUrMJuw4 @ 00:16:52]. Whale Slots puts consumer stream delay at 7, 10, even 30 seconds against bookmaker feeds piped over private satellite links and dedicated stadium fiber, so a goal can already be priced 15 to 20 seconds before the viewer even sees the breakaway [QpjzafRRmjQ @ 00:01:54]. OddsJam's live-betting host reinforces the speed tax from the arb side: live plays get pulled mid-click, 'boom it gets suspended,' and you will miss opportunities even with the play loaded and nothing done wrong [36K9qpRjKXQ @ 00:01:03]. Unabated's Jack frames the same gap as adverse selection: a resting offer in a close fourth quarter only gets filled after a big play turns it into a bad bet [rrKRhjye1sw @ 00:08:09]. Nobody in this group claims a phone-and-stream operator wins the live race on reaction speed alone.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The tool stack splits cleanly into paid terminals and do-it-yourself scanners. Quantitative Predictions ranked five arbitrage tools: EventHub as a free calculator covering Polymarket, Kalshi, and Robinhood; YC-backed Oddspool docked for covering only Polymarket, Kalshi, and Opinion; Arb Bets at about $59 with Novig added; Prediction Hunt at number two; and Predictify on top for 15-plus venues, zero platform fees, and auto-calculating when larger capital would lose money on book depth [He2ctf0VZZ8 @ 00:05:46]. OngPredicts pulled Predictify's pricing page live, showing terminal access from the Builder plan at $48.88 a month and Pro at $149 with 2 million credits, and noted the EV, no-vig, and Kelly calculators are free without sign-in [T6thRudYjsg @ 00:07:35]. Juiced Bets pays for arbs.xyz instead: one click buys both legs in the right ratio, Telegram or Discord pings fire when the pair turns sellable, and the discounted rate is $997 a year against roughly $4,000 before, framed as $2 to $3 a day to make 50 to 250 bucks a day [PaQjSUCZVb0 @ 00:13:01]. At the zero-dollar end, Odds Breaker built a sportsbook scanner on The Odds API's 500 free monthly requests across 47 leagues and flagged five live arbs, including a 2.3% margin on the Derek Lewis MMA fight [aZvtaObt8Gw @ 00:01:27].

Sizing is where the headline spread dies or survives. Chen Trading walks a Mark Kelly 2028 nominee pair, YES near 2 cents on Polymarket and NO just under 90 cents on Opinion for roughly 92 cents combined, and the calculator at $100 shows about 107.75 shares, a 92.8-cent average, roughly 94 cents in fees, and $7.75 net, about 7.8%; the depth rule is that if only 100 shares sit at the 2-cent ask and you need 500, the other 400 fill at higher asks or not at all [lYFPEQllQOw @ 00:03:36]. Taf's terminal capped a Kalshi and Polymarket AI-benchmark pair at roughly $205 to $220 for about $31 profit, warning that pushing more capital earns less because the book is not deep enough [GLvhRHB7n2U @ 00:09:16]. Clark Knows Ball's cross-venue arb on an Austin Ekeler touchdown prop, $11 on Kalshi at +940 against $100 on Chalkboard at -526, netted $5.71, a 4.89% guaranteed return, scaling to $37.84 at $57 and $500 [ghCIWcXbadk @ 00:06:24]. OddsJam's arb tutorial runs the identical ratio logic: $43 staked returns $2 at 4.44%, while $1,720 in returns $1,800 for $80, which is why the green Twitter calendars come from bankroll size rather than a different edge [bKaCBMQuXgk @ 00:05:26].

Operators who build their own pipelines describe the same skeleton. Part Time Larry's Python bot polls ESPN's unofficial site.web.api-espn.com endpoint with a 2-second delay to dodge rate limits, parses the win probability array, subscribes to Kalshi's websocket for live bid and ask on KXNFLGAME tickers, and fires a configurable spike trigger; at a 3% spike it simulated a Seattle YES buy with exits at 95 cents or a timeout, and the position scratched at break-even, possibly down a commission [bA_NUrMJuw4 @ 00:15:10]. Scrape Atlas wires its own scraping API into ChatGPT as a custom MCP plugin for a first version, then says serious operators should offload to a Mac Mini or preferably a Hetzner server to scrape more frequently, still routing through a bot-protection bypass because generic scrapers get blocked [OPiw3RZFInQ @ 00:05:03]. Juiced Bets notes arbs.xyz refreshes every 2 to 3 seconds, so when five people chase the same gap the row simply updates and the bet is gone [PaQjSUCZVb0 @ 00:10:14]. OddsJam's live-betting desk turns off pure live and works the stoppage filter, halftime and commercial breaks, arguing it buys far more time to attack arbitrage plays than in-play markets allow [36K9qpRjKXQ @ 00:05:06].

callout.title: Edges the scanners will not hand you
callout.body: Operator habits the practitioners use to keep accounts clean, capital moving, and scanner noise filtered out before money goes in.
items: Never add change to a stake: a $50.40 leg is a red flag that reads as arbitrage to the books, so round to $50 or $51 and bet in zeros and fives to blend in with casual bettors, giving up maybe a dollar or two of profit [OddsJam: Sports Betting Strategy & Education — bKaCBMQuXgk @ 00:06:52].

Do not lock capital for months: cash out both legs when the Kalshi and Polymarket lines cross over; the Taylor Swift top Spotify artist market crossed roughly every 2 weeks [Juiced Bets — PaQjSUCZVb0 @ 00:08:30].

Treat an outlier price as a reason to check, not to buy: trust the venue with the most money traded, which is how a 22-cent Dodgers gap collapsed to about a third of a cent [OngPredicts — T6thRudYjsg @ 00:02:51].

Anchor live positive EV to Pinnacle as the sharpest book and hunt for totals on FanDuel, DraftKings, or Fliff that are off by a point and a half or more [OddsJam: Sports Betting Strategy & Education — 36K9qpRjKXQ @ 00:09:13].

sop_steps.title: Filter the scanner list
sop_steps.action: Set closing time under 30 days and liquidity above $100,000, then skip rows marked ended or showing a 0-cent side.
sop_steps.detail: A 0-cent side usually means that venue has no real price at all, and the filter keeps cash from being tied up for months in thin venues [OngPredicts — T6thRudYjsg @ 00:01:48].

sop_steps.title: Verify both rule sets settle identically
sop_steps.action: Open the full rules on both venues and compare event, deadline, candidate, and resolution source.
sop_steps.detail: For nomination markets, check how each venue handles a candidate dropping out, a replacement nominee, a delayed convention, or a cancellation; if the wording is unclear, skip the pair [Chen Trading — lYFPEQllQOw @ 00:04:33].

sop_steps.title: Size to the order book, not the headline
sop_steps.action: Enter your intended position size and watch average price, fees, and net profit update on both legs.
sop_steps.detail: A deep book on one side does not fix a thin book on the other, and if the expected edge disappears at your intended size, pass on the trade [Chen Trading — lYFPEQllQOw @ 00:04:15].

sop_steps.title: Fire both legs and hedge any miss
sop_steps.action: Keep enough funds in both wallets, place both sides, then inspect fills before walking away.
sop_steps.detail: If Polymarket fills and the Kalshi price moves before your second leg, the tool tells you how much to place on the Kalshi side to stay hedged rather than exposed to one outcome [Juiced Bets — PaQjSUCZVb0 @ 00:10:30].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split among these operators is whether a retail operator can win on speed at all. Part Time Larry wired the unofficial ESPN Game Cast feed into a Kalshi websocket bot and concluded that the professional algorithmic traders on Kalshi "probably have the fastest data feed and are moving first," confirming on a second game that Kalshi odds moved before his signal [bA_NUrMJuw4 @ 00:03:57]. His verdict is blunt: anyone betting off what they see on TV is "basically wasting their time," so either own the fastest data or a better pre-game model and stop competing on speed [bA_NUrMJuw4 @ 00:17:23]. Clark Knows Ball pitches the reverse thesis for live Kalshi action, arguing in-game opportunities get "even more sporadic" and bigger because you are up against real people in the heat of the moment, not FanDuel and DraftKings conglomerates running algorithms every second [ghCIWcXbadk @ 00:03:15]. Unabated's Jack cuts against that: Kalshi, Polymarket and others use institutional market makers whose algorithms and automated systems essentially act as the bookie, so "if you think it's always going to be you versus some bro on Robin Hood, you're mistaken." He does concede that prime-time screens fly by with recreational tickets mostly under $100, which is why big events can price slightly better than a sportsbook [rrKRhjye1sw @ 00:09:17].

The second fault line is what to do with capital once both legs are on. Juiced Bets refuses to sit in long-dated arbs: on a J.D. Vance election market he does not want money "tied up for the next 2 years," so he waits for Kalshi and Polymarket prices to cross over and cashes out both sides early, citing an aliens-before-2027 pair bought at 14 and 76 cents that crossed and closed for 10% a couple of hours later [PaQjSUCZVb0 @ 00:03:59]. He even rates a Taylor Swift top-Spotify-artist market that crossed roughly every two weeks as a fantastic candidate, because that overlap history makes another cross likely [PaQjSUCZVb0 @ 00:08:30]. Bet The Math's Alex runs the opposite rhythm: pair a Kalshi leg with a sportsbook leg on a single game, and "the second the game ends, you get your money back," which he calls daily compounding [nOjpng5gNGo @ 00:06:57]. OngPredicts enforces the same discipline mechanically, filtering closing time under 30 days and liquidity above $100,000 so cash is not locked for months and thin venues drop out [T6thRudYjsg @ 00:01:48]. Juiced Bets' bet is that these markets "are not efficient" and will keep crossing; the short-dated camp simply collects at the final whistle.

Tooling splits into build and buy camps. Odds Breaker, who tells viewers to stop paying hundreds a month for scanners, builds a free one on the Odds API's 500 free monthly requests with four commands to an AI coder, and it surfaced five live arbs including a 2.3% MMA margin [aZvtaObt8Gw @ 00:00:40]. Scrape Atlas builds the Kalshi-Polymarket monitor inside ChatGPT through the ScrapeAtlas MCP plugin and argues against stretching thin across 50 bets: find one deviating bet and "literally just spam it over" until it materializes [OPiw3RZFInQ @ 00:04:50]. He then pushes serious operators off ChatGPT onto a Mac Mini or a Hetzner server for a faster scraping clip, still routed through ScrapeAtlas because generic scrapers get blocked [OPiw3RZFInQ @ 00:05:03]. The buy camp runs the other way. OngPredicts pays $48.88 a month for Predictify because manual tab-hopping across Polymarket, Kalshi and Opinion means "doing the job of a software myself," yet he insists "I'm not using this to blindly click on every trade that shows up" — the scanner only nominates candidates for research [to-RcU1_UCQ @ 00:03:42]. His filter is simple: a fat spread with basically no liquidity gets skipped, while a smaller spread with real size is potentially more interesting.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Part Time Larry is candid: he ran the ESPN-to-Kalshi bot live during Seahawks versus 49ers and "lost money, but I'm showing it anyway" [bA_NUrMJuw4 @ 00:05:01]. The trade log shows why. His config simulated a YES buy on Seattle after a 3% win-probability spike on a Sam Darnold completion, with two exits — 95 cents or a time stop — and the position auto-exited at break even, where "maybe we even lost money on a commission" [bA_NUrMJuw4 @ 00:15:32]. He also polled ESPN with a 2-second delay to avoid rate limits, on a free feed that "might be 15 seconds, it might be 30 seconds" behind courtsiders and the Sportradar-partnered feeds he figures top Kalshi traders pay up to $5,000 a month for. Whale Slots frames the same trap from the bettor's chair: streams run 7, 10, even 30 seconds late, and a goal can hit the book's feed 15 to 20 seconds before you even see the breakaway [QpjzafRRmjQ @ 00:01:54]. They also flag latency arbitrage, where provider algorithms accept a delayed bet just as the odds shift against you or reject it outright, and their fix is to drop pure reaction betting because by the time you see it, the edge is probably gone [QpjzafRRmjQ @ 00:02:58].

Phantom spreads are the first trap scanner users report. OngPredicts opened a Dodgers World Series row showing 7 cents against 29 cents, a 22-cent gap, and found it was "really about a third of a cent" once the compare tab pulled live prices [T6thRudYjsg @ 00:02:51]. His rule: trust the venue with the most money traded and treat a price far from everyone else as a reason to check, not a reason to buy. Re-running three more top rows about four hours later went "three for three": every gap came from a venue with no live price or a price that had already moved [T6thRudYjsg @ 00:04:11]. Even real spreads shrink with size. Taf's AI-benchmark pair, 6 cents YES on Kalshi against 78 cents NO on Polymarket, returned about $31 at $205 to $220, and "the higher you put, you're actually going to make less money" because the book is not deep enough [GLvhRHB7n2U @ 00:09:16]. Chen Trading spells out the arithmetic: if the first ask is 2 cents with only 100 shares and you need 500, that level covers one-fifth of the order and the rest climbs the book or stays unfilled, so average every level before trusting the two-leg estimate [lYFPEQllQOw @ 00:03:36].

The last traps are contract mismatch, leg risk, idle cash and fees. Taf warns that markets "can be titled the same, they might resolve totally differently, and you will end up losing your money on one of the legs" [GLvhRHB7n2U @ 00:05:51]. Chen Trading's nomination checklist, covering a candidate dropping out, a replacement nominee, a delayed convention or a cancellation, exists because any uncovered case leaves a gap in exposure, and execution adds its own risk: one leg may fill while the other moves or only partially fills [lYFPEQllQOw @ 00:05:14]. His countermeasure is to set maximum total cost and size in advance, then inspect filled shares and average price after each order and recalculate the remaining leg. Odds Breaker names the logistics risk plainly: without cash already sitting in six betting apps ready to fire instantly, the lines can move against you pretty quickly [aZvtaObt8Gw @ 00:01:49]. Unabated's Jack ranks fees as the number-one caveat: a 3% commission can turn a price 5 cents better than DraftKings into a worse bet than you would have had at DraftKings [rrKRhjye1sw @ 00:10:27]. Fees may come off winning wagers, off takers only, or off makers and takers alike, and either way they have to be factored in.

chapters.question_prompt: What separates winning prediction-market traders and trading teams from the losing majority, and how do they run their operation?
chapters.title: Inside the Pro Prediction-Market Desk
chapters.subtitle: Microstructure of wealth transfer across 72M Kalshi trades, three years of Polymarket data, $286-to-$1M and $100-to-$1M case studies, quant and fully manual strategies, building trading teams and tech, political/Iran market analysis, Gen Z trading firms, and sports-betting tax treatment for pros
chapters.executive_summary: Pro prediction-market desks agree the edge is structural: retail buys emotional YES longshots, makers harvest them, and exchanges do not limit winners. Becker's 72M-trade Kalshi dataset shows 5-cent contracts winning 4.18% of the time and makers earning about +2.5% per trade, while only 22% of markets resolve YES. Street mechanics run from Clay's fully manual first-touchdown quoting at about $3K per primetime game and roughly 10% ROI on $60M volume, to Steven's RFQ combo desk where 40-plus NFL makers make five milliseconds decisive. InGenius by Veritasium finds market makers averaging $11,831 versus $3,243 for skilled winners. Disagreements center on taking versus making, with Steven still earning 7-8% taking against 2-3% making, on whether copying RFQ quotes works, and on whether competition has flipped the edge toward YES.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The loudest point of agreement across the desk is that retail order flow carries a structural YES and longshot bias that pros harvest. Jonathan Becker's dataset of 72 million Kalshi trades, walked through by Part Time Larry, shows 5-cent contracts actually winning only 4.18% of the time, while NO bought at 94 cents wins 95% of the time [vT0qMNgOkxo @ 00:04:34]. Larry's own Rockets YES bought at 7% sank to 4%, turning $43 into $24, and the summary is blunt: usually the boring outcome wins, nothing ever happens [vT0qMNgOkxo @ 00:16:37]. Larry calls late cheap YES buying pouring money into a dead bet. Three Markets lands in the same place: fabiano.soul's count shows only 22% of markets resolve YES, and the play is buying NO early in a 90/10 market because it tends to drift to 95/5 [DvHXWcq2iWc @ 00:02:17]. Semi, profiled with P&L over $1M from a $286 deposit in June 2024, calls the approach reverse stupidity: fading sensationalism bias. InGenius by Veritasium's three-year Polymarket study adds that the skilled winners, roughly 3% of accounts, avoid overpriced longshots and favour favourites [CTUqmUHvd2Y @ 00:20:52]. The shared rule: treat emotional YES buying as the flow you trade against.

Second consensus point: live on the maker side of the book. Becker's data shows makers earning about +2.5% excess return per trade while takers lose about the same, and Reichenbach and Walther (2025) found the identical split on Polymarket [vT0qMNgOkxo @ 00:05:36]. Becker's own custom NBA script found roughly $7M in taker losses. InGenius by Veritasium measured skilled directional winners averaging $3,243 of profit over two years against $11,831 for market makers, with the top 0.1% of accounts acting as makers about half the time [CTUqmUHvd2Y @ 00:22:13]. The working pros on Inside Prediction Markets back it with their own books. Clay, the fully manual trader out of Princeton, New Jersey, runs 80-85% maker and calls the process completely manual [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:12:30]. Steven, the part-time market maker who crossed $1M in P&L, flipped from 95% taking in January to roughly 20% taking and 80% making, mostly RFQs on combos plus niche markets such as NASCAR. The nuance the pros add is that making is the volume engine, not automatically the fattest margin: Steven still books about 7-8% ROI taking against 2-3% making, and the taking P&L still leads the account [ieRL4BXtMGA @ 00:06:55]. Making buys scale; selective taking still pays the bills.

The third pillar is venue logic: sharps migrated because prediction markets take their action instead of cutting them off. Troy Cooks of OddsJam, a pro for two to three years who made over $250K in 2025, puts it simply: sportsbooks hate winners, while peer-to-peer exchanges like Novig charge fees and could care less how much you profit [zMU9NWt0gdE @ 00:02:38]. Cooks also pitches these as the newest and least efficient markets, with insider flow visible because every portfolio is public, and reports about $20K in 30 days from arbitrage, +EV and the tool. Steven adds that offshore books are in a slow death of limits, slow pay and 15-second timers [ieRL4BXtMGA @ 00:12:00]. NBC News frames the structural driver: CFTC federal oversight lets users in even where sports gambling is illegal, while sportsbooks carry large capital reserves and tight regulation, and the segment's critic warns the regulatory gate is completely down [APN3zwcwPdQ @ 00:01:52]. Where to hunt is also agreed: Becker's data flags entertainment, crypto and sports as inefficient and finance as efficient [vT0qMNgOkxo @ 00:12:34]. The baseline prerequisite is cultural as much as technical: think like the casino, diversify across a large number of bets, and accept that longshots sometimes hit.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Clay's first-touchdown playbook is the most granular manual workflow on the desk. Quote the top 10 players, price the team without the ball at the pregame line minus about 4 cents for roughly 5% ROI per player, refill in 900-contract lots, and before each snap drop the team with the ball to 1 cent before repricing after the play [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:14:55]. The take runs about $3K per primetime game, net negative in only two or three games a year, but Clay got courtsided at 4,000 contracts and 95 cents and now says that edge is dead [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:18:24]. The live focus has shifted to end-of-game football, the highest-ROI window because people have no idea what they're doing, plus hockey, tennis, soccer and Chinese basketball. Clay listens to referee audio rather than trusting sportsbook data feeds. Liquidity has transformed underneath all of it: early Kalshi college football spreads were 3-4 cents wide, and now roughly $70K sits at a 1-cent spread [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:10:42]. Novig goes further, with Henry and Chris pointing to 300-500K-contract walls quoted a penny wide with no fees [ZmMVHubZpns @ 00:06:04]. Clay pegs fair margins at 2-4% live and 1-2% pregame, and says landing in a 5% range is quite profitable.

Steven's RFQ operation shows how fast quoting edges compress. RFQ started at the end of May, the World Cup made June and July easy, and from August competitors began offering 0.1% hold, pushing the focus to latency and combo quoting [ieRL4BXtMGA @ 00:08:22]. Pricing is about 80% top down, and some NFL markets carry 40-plus makers, so being five milliseconds behind means getting nothing [ieRL4BXtMGA @ 00:22:05]. Steven expects proprietary pricing to matter within three to four months, because low-hold SGP quotes suggest rivals originate their own numbers. The build is one developer working with Steven for nine months, because Steven's own builds were garbage, with developers originally sourced through coaching calls. Michael Hoffman, head of engineering on the Inside Prediction Markets trading team, came from StoneX FIX connectivity into about 100 exchanges, hires for distributed systems and messaging-bus skills, and discounts big-tech candidates [4UVkZUKEmPI @ 00:35:53]. Clay runs the opposite stack: no models, intuition only, and no appetite for troubleshooting, which makes tooling cost a real line item. Multi-venue order-book software runs about $0.02 per contract, tiered, which on Clay's roughly $5M a month of volume would cost more than $10K [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:25:32]. Hoffman stays black boxed from pricing entirely, walling engineering off from the trading book.

The contract math is simple. Event contracts pay $1 or $0, so YES at 67 cents plus NO at 33 cents equals a dollar, and InGenius by Veritasium's spread-capture template is to model 67% fair value, bid YES at 65 cents and NO at 31 cents, pay 96 cents and lock 4 cents, with the risk that only one side fills [CTUqmUHvd2Y @ 00:23:49]. The same team flags multi-outcome arbitrage, buying all YES for under $1 or all NO for under $2 in a three-outcome market, and notes the top 0.1% average more than 2,300 trades a day against a median of 78. On the taker side, Troy Cooks prices a 60-cent contract as returning 40 cents of profit and says OddsJam's Prediction Traders Tool, running the Sniper 2.0 model at a $250 average bet and about 10 bets a day, is pitched at +$5,000 over 30 days via copy trading [zMU9NWt0gdE @ 00:04:45]. For vetting traders, the Inside Prediction Markets team uses a distribution-based CLV band, checks sizing against optimal Kelly, and demands live results inside their own system rather than backtests [xM4qzY2FKFw @ 00:29:10]. Tax mechanics matter too: SharpMoney's Gary Conler notes Kalshi's terms call its contracts 1256 contracts, which would make profits capital gains outside the 90% loss rule [O3v0_n4fZLQ @ 00:22:29].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split on the desk is whether 'just bet NO' is still an edge or already a crowded trade. Part Time Larry runs the 'nothing ever happens' playbook straight off 72 million Kalshi fills: pick emotional categories, target 5 to 10 cent longshots, buy the NO side as a resting maker limit, and spread the book across many bets [vT0qMNgOkxo @ 00:15:33]. Three Markets backs the bias with Fabiano.soul's stat that only 22% of markets resolve YES, and Andrew Lonardi wants to buy the entire index of NOs, yet the same hosts float the counterpoint that degens hammering the 10 cent side may already offset the YES lean [DvHXWcq2iWc @ 00:04:39]. Clay, who has pushed roughly $60M in manual volume, goes further and says competition has flipped the edge toward YES on the sports ladders they trade [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:29:30]. InGenius splits the difference: its skilled-winner cohort avoids overpriced longshots and leans toward favourites rather than blanket-shorting every headline [CTUqmUHvd2Y @ 00:20:52]. The operator read is that the NO tilt is real in emotional, entertainment, crypto and sports categories but needs to be re-measured per venue and per season, because the practitioners who live in liquid sports ladders already see the premium being competed away by other makers.

Making versus taking is the second fault line, and the numbers do not line up neatly. Part Time Larry's Kalshi data shows makers earning roughly 2.5% excess return per trade while takers bleed about the same, a pattern Reichenbach and Walther also found on Polymarket [vT0qMNgOkxo @ 00:05:36]. InGenius lands on the same side: market makers in its sample averaged $11,831 versus $3,243 for other skilled winners, and the top 0.1% are makers about half the time [CTUqmUHvd2Y @ 00:22:13]. Clay runs 80 to 85% maker flow and does it completely by hand, quoting ladders on intuition rather than a model [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:12:30]. Steven complicates the story: their book has swung from 95% taking in January to about 80% making, mostly RFQs on combos and niche markets like NASCAR, yet taking still prints the bigger PnL at a 7 to 8% ROI against only 2 to 3% on the making side [ieRL4BXtMGA @ 00:06:55]. The practical split: making supplies steady, thinner margin while live taking is where Steven still books the fat edges, and they run both rather than picking one. Anyone copying maker returns from aggregate studies should expect thinner per-trade margins once forty competing quoters show up.

The remaining arguments are about desk structure and where the big money sits. On the Novig episode, Chris argues the true end bosses stay offshore out of tax and habit [ZmMVHubZpns @ 00:23:41], while Henry counters that it is really stranded offshore and crypto balances keeping them there, and adds that prediction markets let multiple millions go down quietly [ZmMVHubZpns @ 00:27:08]. On building the team, Larry wants a named head for each sport for accountability, topped up with generalists and part-time specialists for Grand Slams and F1, whereas Joe prefers a quant-firm stack of generalist traders, developers and researchers [xM4qzY2FKFw @ 00:19:36]. Politics produces the sharpest live trade dispute: Gavin says pundits underplay tails like a 55 to 56 seat Democratic Senate and wants to buy tail Democrats such as Turek in Iowa rather than Talarico at 76, while a host pushes back that with Democrats at 75% for the Senate, 55 to 56 seats cannot be the likely outcome [4UVkZUKEmPI @ 00:16:43]. Gavin narrows the claim to the underdog Democrats being slightly underpriced, not the favourite. Gavin also warns that market makers should fear correlation in political parlays, and few political RFQ trades get done at all.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive mistakes on this desk come from contract wording, not pricing. Steven misread the weather resolution rule on a NASCAR pole-position market and lost about $35K, calling it the single most expensive mistake of their career [ieRL4BXtMGA @ 00:38:21]. Clay took a similar hit on cricket after misreading a 19.5 versus 18.5 line on a player who went on to score about 100 [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:36:20]. Venue rules diverge even on the same event: on the Bermuda Open, Novig voided bets while Kalshi let them stand, which turns an identical position into a live bet on one screen and a void on another [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:06:02]. The Inside Prediction Markets team flags this as a structural staffing cost, because trading Novig, Kalshi and Polymarket at once means handling different rules on each, and every new league added, from F1 to NASCAR, needs more people watching it [xM4qzY2FKFw @ 00:15:52]. The check before any size goes on: read the resolution source, the void conditions and the exact line on every venue in the hedge, and do not trade a market whose rules you cannot explain in one sentence.

Edges on this desk decay fast, and the practitioners name the dates. Clay's first-touchdown ladder, quoting the top ten players at the pregame line minus about 4 cents for roughly 5% ROI each, earned about $3K per primetime game until they got courtsided at 4,000 contracts at 95 cents; they now say that edge is dead [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:18:24]. Clay also dropped 61K in a single week betting against the Knicks, a reminder that a 10% lifetime ROI on about $60M of volume still carries ugly weeks [tM5MKtoBoZ0 @ 00:20:35]. Steven's RFQ book coasted through the World Cup in June and July, then from August competitors started quoting a 0.1% hold, compressing edges and forcing the shift into latency and combo quoting [ieRL4BXtMGA @ 00:08:22]. Chris ran the defensive answer, quoting only at a 10%-plus margin early and absorbing late flow, and still lost the McGregor versus Holloway example running it [ZmMVHubZpns @ 00:35:23]. The economics check is to log ROI per strategy per month, because each of these traders found out the edge had closed only after a costly fill, and the next liquidity crunch on island and playoff games is already expected.

The back office is where profitable traders quietly bleed. Gary Conler stresses that the 90% rule cuts losses, not winnings, so $1M won against $1.1M lost still leaves taxable income, and they watched a client report $1.2M of W2Gs while IRS records showed $3.7M [O3v0_n4fZLQ @ 00:13:56]. Andrew McMillan of REH CPA adds the recreational trap: losses only count if you itemize, capped at winnings, and you cannot net wins against losses at all [rN19s1QAAYo @ 00:01:24]. Custody is the second leak: after the Polymarket international front-end hack and the Binance compromise rumor, the Inside Prediction Markets hosts concluded never to keep money on an exchange, while admitting hot wallets are needed to trade [4UVkZUKEmPI @ 00:09:20]. Automation is no shortcut either: InGenius built a weather market-making bot with $103 and finished six days down $21.50, warning that professional firms have better infrastructure and network connections [CTUqmUHvd2Y @ 00:29:19]. The reconciliation check is to tie every return to the IRS wage and income totals, keep session records both ways until attorneys sign off, and hedge each book toward zero at year end.

chapters.question_prompt: Which regulated prediction-market venues exist, how do they differ from sportsbooks, and how do brokers like Interactive Brokers deliver event contracts?
chapters.title: The Venue Map: Kalshi, ForecastEx & Brokered Event Contracts
chapters.subtitle: Prediction markets vs sportsbooks, top 10 venues, Kalshi founders and COO on the business, Kalshi Pro, ForecastEx buy-only design and hedging economic and climate risk, trading Kalshi/CME/ForecastEx inside IBKR, geopolitics contracts, and the critique of prediction markets as gambling
chapters.executive_summary: Across Kalshi, ForecastEx and the IBKR brokered terminal, practitioners agree the product is a binary contract priced between roughly 1 and 99 cents that reads directly as probability and settles at $1 or $0, with prices set peer-to-peer rather than by a house. The street mechanics are tight: ForecastEx pairs Yes and No at $1.01 for a half-penny-per-side fee, Kalshi routed through IBKR costs $0.02 per contract, early exits double the fee load, and ForecastEx pays a variable coupon quoted at 3.14, 3.38, 4.3 and 4.33 percent. Venue routing splits macro (CPI, Fed) toward ForecastEx or CME and sports, elections and culture toward Kalshi. Disagreements are sharp: Kalshi's COO says there is no house, while The Young Turks cite 79-84% losing accounts and Peterffy calls ForecastEx's US clearinghouse probably safer.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The baseline every venue operator agrees on is simple: a prediction-market contract is a Yes/No claim priced between roughly 1 and 99 cents that settles at $1 if right and $0 if wrong, and that price reads directly as probability. Trade Handle frames it with Yes at 60 cents and No near 40 cents, settling at $1 or $0, with traders rather than an operator setting the number peer-to-peer [LHwUBaFR_no @ 00:00:57]. Simple Betting Guides makes the same point from the bettor side: sportsbook odds need converting into implied probability, while a 0-to-$1 price already is one [zfqcFKWL2gA @ 00:01:43]. closeuptrading drills it into position math: 10 contracts at 30 cents cost $3, a correct call pays $10 for a $7 gain, and the maximum loss is exactly what was paid [4_swDdRFYJc @ 00:00:16]. Kalshi's CEO describes the engine as working exactly like the NASDAQ, where a 60-cent buyer collects $1 for a 40-cent profit and the counterparty posts that 40 cents [rDeB10i9gCE @ 00:01:16]. The operator takeaway is that the contract price, not odds, is the key number, and max risk on an unlevered position is the premium paid, whether the ticket routes to Kalshi, ForecastEx or CME.

The second point of agreement is structural: there is no house. Kalshi's CEO argues a sportsbook sets the price, bans and limits winners, and targets losers, while an open marketplace wants winners because winners are the smart people; the test is the structure, not the topic, and the legal base is the Commodity Exchange Act of 1974, where federal uniformity means deeper liquidity and better prices [rDeB10i9gCE @ 00:03:00]. Kalshi's co-founder and COO puts the revenue model bluntly on Schwab Network: sportsbook revenue equals customer losses, whereas Kalshi does not make money when users lose and simply takes a transaction fee [ZW18j-a-TuY @ 00:17:38]. The Interactive Brokers podcast desk echoes it for ForecastEx, saying the venue is not doing a house-edge kind of thing and that the extra penny on a $1.01 pair is the fee, half a penny per side [rMm-V95moXc @ 00:19:06]. Trade Handle adds the regulatory frame operators need before routing anything: sportsbooks sit under gambling law, some prediction markets sit under commodities regulation, and that line is still changing quickly, so legality depends on where the trader lives [LHwUBaFR_no @ 00:03:14]. For a venue map, that means every ticket is a peer-to-peer contract with a disclosed fee, not a wager against an operator's margin.

The third consensus is that venues are not interchangeable and the prerequisites differ by route. TC Trading maps the IBKR terminal as three venues behind one cash account: Kalshi is the consumer venue, CME is institutional, and ForecastEx is IBKR's own exchange, with the desk focus on macro [MREcV1sLqwc @ 00:01:23]. OngPredicts says the first decision is residency: US traders get regulated, dollar-denominated venues with full KYC, while global traders run crypto wallets and stablecoins, and picking wrong means you cannot sign up, cannot trade what you want, or leave better prices elsewhere [4SzgTKdaSHI @ 00:00:49]. On the brokered route, the Interactive Brokers podcast says trading permissions take about a day to switch on [rMm-V95moXc @ 00:15:48], and closeuptrading flags that eligibility is 21+, alongside the thin-market spread risk [4_swDdRFYJc @ 00:02:16]. Stack those together and the baseline kit is a verified account on the right side of the residency line, venue permissions approved before the data print you want to trade, and a clear sense of whether the question is a macro release or a sports, election or culture market, because TC Trading routes CPI and Fed questions to ForecastEx or CME and elections, culture and sports to Kalshi.

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The brokered workflow TC Trading walks through starts inside one IBKR cash account that routes across Kalshi, CME and ForecastEx with smart order routing to the best price; the path is Trade, then IBKR Prediction Markets [MREcV1sLqwc @ 00:00:53]. Before sizing anything, the speaker clicks show market rules, which links an 8-page full rules document, then places a limit order: an initial bid at 38 cents, then a fill at 39 cents for 100 contracts, with Day or IOC as the time-in-force choices [MREcV1sLqwc @ 00:05:39]. The fill immediately showed an average price of 41 cents because of 2 cents in fees, so unrealized P&L opened at minus $2 on the fill itself [MREcV1sLqwc @ 00:07:38]. closeuptrading explains why the limit order matters: Yes at 65 cents plus No at 36 cents totals $1.01, the extra cent is the spread, and in thin markets a market order pays a wide spread, so limits are the default on every venue [4_swDdRFYJc @ 00:00:56]. The same speaker reads exits differently by venue: on Kalshi you sell, on ForecastEx you buy the opposite side, and trading the probability itself, buying at 30 and selling at 45, captures 15 cents without waiting for settlement.

Fees are where the venues actually separate. Interactive Brokers' ForecastEx explainer sets the pair at half a penny per side, so Yes plus No bids total $1.01, with no other exchange, clearing, data or brokerage charges, and pricing data is free [ceR-weGZSXc @ 00:01:53]. TC Trading prices the brokered alternatives: ForecastEx at $0.01 built into the $1.01, Kalshi at $0.02 split as one cent IBKR plus one cent exchange, and CME at a cent plus pass-through fees on larger notional [MREcV1sLqwc @ 00:11:23]. There are no settlement fees, but exiting early doubles the fee load: a 48-cent exit nets about 46 cents, roughly $5 on 100 contracts, which the speaker says will definitely eat into profits, while warning the fee numbers may change [MREcV1sLqwc @ 00:12:10]. On the other side of the ledger, ForecastEx pays an incentive coupon on positions held overnight; the Interactive Brokers podcast quotes it at 4.33% annualized, the same rate IBKR pays on idle cash, and says it adjusts with the mark, so a CPI contract moving from 52 cents toward 80 or 90 cents earns on the higher value [rMm-V95moXc @ 00:03:15]. Per those numbers, holding to settlement avoids the second fee leg; scalping the probability pays fees twice.

ForecastEx's buy-only design changes exit math, and three IBKR-side voices run the numbers. The ForecastEx explainer shows the close-out: hold Yes at 26 cents, buy No at 31 cents, total cost 57 cents against a $1 netting, a 43-cent profit; the ugly version is No at 70 plus Yes at 86, $1.56 in for $1 out, a 56-cent loss before coupons [ceR-weGZSXc @ 00:06:14]. ForecastEx CEO Downey frames it as buying No at 31 being roughly equivalent to selling Yes at 70, and any pair that nets below $1 pays out, with no novation needed because Yes and No are separate contracts [Vix7rchq6b8 @ 00:11:37]. Thomas Peterffy gives the simplest case: Yes at 40 plus No at 40 is 80 cents for a $1 payout [GaBqUuuLjrQ @ 00:08:02]. For hedgers, Kalshi's CEO supplies the template: an ice cream shop makes $100 on a sunny day and loses $100 on a cold one, so buying 200 cold-weather contracts at 10 percent costs $20 and locks in plus $80 whichever way the weather breaks [rDeB10i9gCE @ 00:08:54]. The pattern is consistent across venues: size the opposing contract count to the dollar exposure, pay the premium up front, and the outcome range collapses to a known number.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split is whether this is a market or a casino with a federal license. The Young Turks call it flatly: “it’s gambling,” just with less regulation, sitting under the CFTC instead of state gambling law and live in all 50 states [Y-ToFo3PvAw @ 00:00:35]. They back it with return data: the median prediction-market return runs -8%, worse than -5% at sportsbooks and -6.55% on slots [Y-ToFo3PvAw @ 00:06:37]. Kalshi’s CEO, speaking with Natalie Fratto, draws the line somewhere else entirely: the test is open marketplace versus the house, and “It’s a structure. It’s not the topic” [rDeB10i9gCE @ 00:05:06]. Kalshi’s co-founder on Schwab Network makes the incentive argument directly: a sportsbook’s revenue equals customer losses, while Kalshi says “We don’t make money when users lose” and takes a transaction fee instead [ZW18j-a-TuY @ 00:17:38]. Evan at centsorsense sits between the camps, calling the product “kind of like a coin toss” and “akin to gambling” unless the position is hedging a real exposure, the way flood insurance offsets a house [qH8nQqkMNv8 @ 00:06:43]. The operator takeaway: the same contract reads as a hedge or a wager depending on whether an offsetting exposure exists outside the account.

Practitioners also split on which venue is structurally safer. CryptoCoins host Daniel J. Glenn pitches Kalshi as the “first CFTC regulated” prediction site, onshore, with protections comparable to a stock platform [1v9Cq8L6jqg @ 00:05:52]. Thomas Peterffy, speaking to John Lothian News, pushes back hard: Kalshi leans on a “foreign corporation” as guarantor, while ForecastEx clears through a US clearinghouse and is, in Peterffy’s words, “probably safer” [GaBqUuuLjrQ @ 00:02:35]. ForecastEx CEO Downey, on the IBKR podcast, frames the design gap: Yes and No are separate contracts that never share a price, paired at $1.01, making it “the first derivative in the world that doesn’t go into a Clearing House requiring Novation” [Vix7rchq6b8 @ 00:04:05]. The two designs force different exit playbooks. closeuptrading spells it out: on Kalshi you simply sell; on ForecastEx you exit by buying the opposite side, and trading the probability means buying at 30¢ and getting out at 45¢ for a 15¢ gain [4_swDdRFYJc @ 00:01:16]. Downey gives the ForecastEx translation: buying No at 31 is roughly the same as selling Yes at 70 [Vix7rchq6b8 @ 00:11:37]. Operators running both venues need two mental models: a two-sided book on Kalshi and a buy-only pairing engine on ForecastEx.

Even the headline ForecastEx incentive coupon gets quoted differently depending on who is talking and when. TC Trading reads the interest at 3.14 APY on the IBKR ticket [MREcV1sLqwc @ 00:10:26], closeuptrading lists the coupon at 3.38% per year and flags it as variable [4_swDdRFYJc @ 00:01:33], Peterffy cites 4.3% paid on the daily closing price [GaBqUuuLjrQ @ 00:04:25], and the Cents of Security podcast puts it at 4.33% annualized, matching what IBKR pays on idle cash [rMm-V95moXc @ 00:03:15]. The rate floats, so any coupon number in a pitch is a snapshot. The coupon also reshapes holding periods. Peterffy argues it makes long-dated questions such as national debt above $66T by 2035 viable, and that interest on an appreciated price can exceed the $1 win itself [GaBqUuuLjrQ @ 00:04:25]. The podcast adds that the coupon adjusts with the mark, so a CPI contract climbing from 52¢ to 80–90¢ earns more as it runs [rMm-V95moXc @ 00:13:29]. TC Trading treats venue choice as a category call rather than a yield call: CPI and Fed questions go to ForecastEx or CME, while elections, culture and sports belong on Kalshi [MREcV1sLqwc @ 00:13:05].
